title: Sermones Suppositi. Classis IIII. De Diversis
author: Augustinus (pseudo)
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0040a.stoa001d.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.

passages.original: nihil quod inferius superiusque dici possit. Ideo tota dettas sua perfectione a'qualis est; ut, exceptis vorahulis quae proprietatem personarum indicant, quidquid de una persona dicitur, de tribus dignissime possit in- telligi. Atque ut confutantes Arium, unam camdemque dicimus Trinitatis esse substantiam, et unum in tribus personis fatemur Deum : ita impietatem Sabellii declinantes, tres personas expressas sui proprietate distinguimus : non ipsum s;bi Patrem, ipsum Filiuin, ipsum Spiritum unctum esse dicentes;
passages.english: nothing that could be called lower or higher. Therefore the whole Godhead is equal in its perfection, so that, except for the terms that indicate the distinctive property of the persons, whatever is said of one person can most fittingly be understood of the three. And just as, in refuting Arius, we say that the substance of the Trinity is one and the same, and confess one God in three persons, so, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons, marked out by their own distinctive property, not saying that the same one is to himself Father, the same one Son, the same one Holy Spirit;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'dettas' read as deitas, 'a'qualis' as aequalis, 'vorahulis' as vocabulis, 's;bi' as sibi, 'Filiuin' as Filium. 'Spiritum unctum' is evidently a misreading of 'Spiritum sanctum' (Holy Spirit) and is translated so.

passages.original: Nos autem Catholici contra utrumque divinarum Scripturarum auctoritate muniti, adversus Arium veram et perfectam Verbi divinitatem ; adversus Apollinarem perfectam hominis in Christo defendimus veritatem. Itaque sicut contra Arium superiori tractatu perfectionem deitatis asseruimus, ita nunc contra Apolliuarem perfectum hominem comprobamus.
passages.english: But we Catholics, fortified against both by the authority of the divine Scriptures, defend against Arius the true and perfect divinity of the Word, and against Apollinaris the perfect reality of the man in Christ. Accordingly, just as in the preceding treatise we affirmed the perfection of the Godhead against Arius, so now against Apollinaris we demonstrate the perfect man.
